references.text: Jesus' claim to be one with the Father led the Jews to pick up stones to stone him for blasphemy. In a later discussion (John 10:34-36), Jesus uses the statement in Psalms that some are called 'gods' (sons of the Most High) as an argument that it is not blasphemy to call oneself God's Son when Scripture has already called some gods.

In his solemn prayer, Jesus asks that the disciples may be one, just as He and the Father are one. This is a direct theological expansion of the concept of unity from 10:30, where the ontological unity between Father and Son becomes the model for the relational unity between believers and God.

Jesus confirms that to see Him is to see the Father, and that the words He speaks are the Father's words. This underscores the same unity expressed in 10:30, where Jesus and the Father are one in essence and action, so that they cannot be separated in their divine identity.

Jesus justifies his work by stating that the Father is working until now, and He also works. This led the Jews to seek to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father and made himself equal with God. This is a direct precursor to the conflicts surrounding the statement of unity in 10:30.

Jesus declares 'Before Abraham was born, I am', a claim of eternal existence that led the Jews to pick up stones to stone him. This shows the same reaction to Jesus' divine self-understanding as in 10:30, where the claim of unity with the Father is interpreted as a claim to be God.
